trial_name: SEPSISPAM — High vs Low Blood-Pressure Target in Septic Shock (2014)
citation: Asfar P, Meziani F, Hamel JF, et al; SEPSISPAM Investigators. High versus low blood-pressure target in patients with septic shock. N Engl J Med. 2014;370(17):1583-1593.
one_liner: In septic shock, targeting MAP 80–85 mmHg vs 65–70 mmHg did not improve 28-day mortality (36.6% vs 34.0%; HR 1.07) but increased atrial fibrillation (6.7% vs 2.8%); chronic hypertension subgroup had less RRT with higher MAP.

pico.population: Adults with septic shock requiring vasopressors after fluid resuscitation
pico.intervention: High-target MAP strategy: vasopressors titrated to maintain MAP 80–85 mmHg for first 5 days
pico.comparison: Low-target MAP strategy: vasopressors titrated to maintain MAP 65–70 mmHg for first 5 days

background.existing_knowledge: MAP targets in septic shock were largely consensus-driven, commonly set at ≥65 mmHg, with wide practice variation. Physiological rationale supported higher MAP in chronic hypertension and renal hypoperfusion, but higher vasopressor exposure was plausibly harmful.
background.knowledge_gap: Prior evidence consisted mainly of observational associations and small studies; a definitive multicentre trial was needed to balance potential organ-protection against catecholamine-related harms.
background.hypothesis: Targeting a higher MAP (80–85 mmHg) vs lower MAP (65–70 mmHg) would reduce 28-day mortality, and effect may be modified by chronic arterial hypertension.

methods.design: Randomised, multicentre, parallel-group, open-label trial in 29 French ICUs; central computer-based randomisation; prespecified subgroup stratification by chronic arterial hypertension; follow-up to 90 days.

inclusion: Adults with septic shock requiring vasopressors after fluid resuscitation
Enrolled within 6 hours of shock onset
Minimum fluid load of 30 mL/kg (protocol amendment)
exclusion: Catecholamine dose <0.1 µg/kg/min (common reasons for ineligibility)

methods.intervention: High-target MAP strategy: vasopressors titrated to maintain MAP 80–85 mmHg for first 5 days, primarily norepinephrine; weaning per protocolised decrement schedules.
methods.comparison: Low-target MAP strategy: vasopressors titrated to maintain MAP 65–70 mmHg for first 5 days; other vasoactive agents permitted as clinically indicated.
methods.blinding: Open-label; outcomes largely objective (mortality, RRT, prespecified adverse events).
methods.sample_size_power: Planned 800 patients to detect 10% absolute reduction in 28-day mortality (45% to 35%) with 80% power at 5% significance; analysed 776.
secondary_outcomes: Survival without organ support at day 28
Serious adverse events (atrial fibrillation, myocardial infarction)

headline_bullets: 28-day mortality similar: 36.6% high-target vs 34.0% low-target (HR 1.07, 95% CI 0.84–1.38, P=0.57)
High-target increased new-onset atrial fibrillation (6.7% vs 2.8%, P=0.02)
In chronic hypertension subgroup, high-target reduced RRT (31.7% vs 42.2%, P=0.046) and creatinine doubling (38.9% vs 52.0%, P=0.02)

outcomes_table.outcome: Survival at day 28 without organ support
outcomes_table.note: Organ support: vasopressors, mechanical ventilation, or RRT
Patients treated with RRT not included in calculation

outcomes_table.outcome: Newly diagnosed atrial fibrillation (serious adverse event)

outcomes_table.note: Definition: ECG changes + troponin rise + echocardiographic regional wall motion abnormality; angiographic confirmation when possible
Composite of prespecified serious adverse events

subgroup_table.subgroup: Chronic arterial hypertension — Doubling of plasma creatinine

safety: Newly diagnosed atrial fibrillation: 26/388 (6.7%) vs 11/388 (2.8%), P=0.02
Any serious adverse event: 74/388 (19.1%) vs 69/388 (17.8%), P=0.64
High-target group had greater vasopressor exposure (median norepinephrine day 1: 0.58 vs 0.45 µg/kg/min, P<0.001) and longer duration (4.7 vs 3.7 days, P<0.001)

domains.notes: Central computer-based randomisation, allocation concealment, prespecified stratification by chronic hypertension; baseline characteristics balanced (e.g., chronic hypertension 43.0% vs 44.6%; SAPS II 56.1 vs 57.2).
Open-label MAP titration; primary outcome (mortality) objective; secondary outcomes protocol-defined, but potential for co-intervention differences.
798 randomised, 22 excluded post-randomisation (withdrawal of consent/guardianship); primary analysis included 388 per group (ITT).

Target non-adherence: 16.5% high-target vs 10.3% low-target (P=0.01); 3.6% high-target down-titrated due to adverse effects; achieved MAPs slightly above targets (low-target 70–75 mmHg, high-target 85–90 mmHg).
Well-balanced; SAPS II, SOFA, chronic hypertension similar.

internal_validity.verdict: Moderate-to-strong internal validity: robust randomisation and objective outcomes, but open-label design and target non-adherence may dilute treatment effect.

domains.notes: Typical adult ICU septic shock cohort (high severity, ~74–79% mechanically ventilated, ~43–45% chronic hypertension), but exclusively French ICUs.
Generalizable to high-income ICUs using norepinephrine-first strategies with early enrolment; caution in resource-limited settings or different vasopressor formularies.

external_validity.verdict: Good external validity for contemporary high-income ICUs, but limited where baseline practice or achievable MAP control differ substantially.

strengths: Large, pragmatic, multicentre RCT addressing a ubiquitous ICU titration decision
Prespecified subgroup stratification for chronic hypertension
Objective primary outcome with prespecified safety endpoints
Documented separation in vasopressor exposure and achieved MAP between strategies
limitations: Open-label MAP management with potential for performance bias
Common target non-adherence (16.5% high-target, 10.3% low-target) likely biasing toward null
Achieved MAP in low-target arm frequently 70–75 mmHg, narrowing physiological contrast
Final analysed sample size slightly below planned (776 vs 800), and design assumptions for mortality may have overestimated event rate

critical_appraisal.summary: SEPSISPAM is a well-conducted RCT with moderate-to-strong internal validity and good external validity; the neutral mortality result is credible, but the open-label design and target non-adherence may have attenuated a true effect. The chronic hypertension renal signal is hypothesis-generating.

sections.authors_conclusion: Routinely targeting MAP 80–85 mmHg in septic shock did not improve survival compared with 65–70 mmHg, while increasing catecholamine exposure and atrial fibrillation. Among patients with chronic arterial hypertension, higher MAP was associated with less RRT and less creatinine doubling, supporting selective higher MAP targets.

clinical_bottom_line.verdict: Default MAP target of ~65 mmHg is supported; consider higher targets (80–85 mmHg) in patients with chronic hypertension to potentially reduce renal injury, but weigh against increased arrhythmia risk.
clinical_bottom_line.applies_to: Adult ICU patients with septic shock requiring vasopressors, especially those with chronic hypertension.
clinical_bottom_line.does_not_mean: Higher MAP targets are universally harmful; they may benefit renal outcomes in chronic hypertension.
implementation_caveats: Achieved MAP in low-target group often exceeded 65–70 mmHg; real-world 'usual care' may already approximate this
Monitor for atrial fibrillation when targeting higher MAP
Individualise based on renal function and hypertension history

controversies.notes: Highlighted that any benefit of higher MAP would need to outweigh increased vasopressor exposure and arrhythmia/ischaemia risk, and interpreted the chronic hypertension renal signal as plausible but not definitive.
Raised methodological and interpretive issues (including achievable MAP separation and implications for subgroup inference), with author reply clarifying trial conduct and interpretation.
Compared lower (60–65 mmHg) vs higher (75–80 mmHg) MAP targets in vasodilatory shock; established feasibility and suggested clinically meaningful heterogeneity hypotheses for larger trials.
Tested permissive hypotension (MAP 60–65 mmHg) vs usual care in older patients with vasodilatory hypotension; informed the contemporary 'less vasopressor exposure' paradigm alongside SEPSISPAM.
Included SEPSISPAM, OVATION, and 65 Trial; suggested lower MAP targets may reduce 90-day mortality with low certainty and did not identify robust subgroups that clearly benefit from higher targets.

Found no convincing mortality advantage for higher MAP targets in vasodilatory shock; reinforced arrhythmia/cardiac complication concerns, supporting a default lower MAP approach with individualisation.
Major guidelines recommend an initial MAP target around 65 mmHg with individualisation (e.g., chronic hypertension) rather than routine higher targets, based partly on SEPSISPAM.

context_related_trials.relation: Pilot RCT comparing lower (60–65 mmHg) vs higher (75–80 mmHg) MAP targets in vasodilatory shock; informed feasibility and heterogeneity hypotheses.
RCT of permissive hypotension (MAP 60–65 mmHg) vs usual care in older patients with vasodilatory hypotension; supports less vasopressor exposure paradigm.
Suggested lower MAP targets may reduce 90-day mortality with low certainty; no robust subgroup benefiting from higher targets.
No mortality advantage for higher MAP; reinforced arrhythmia concerns; supports default lower MAP with individualisation.

unresolved_questions: Does higher MAP definitively improve renal outcomes in chronic hypertension? (Requires confirmation in dedicated RCT)
What is the optimal MAP target in older patients or those with pre-existing cardiac disease?
Can a strategy of early higher MAP followed by de-escalation balance renal protection and arrhythmia risk?
How do different vasopressor agents (e.g., vasopressin) interact with MAP targets?

quick_recall.one_line_takeaway: Default MAP ~65 mmHg in septic shock; consider higher targets in chronic hypertension for renal protection, but monitor for arrhythmias.
